title: Semantic versioning
idea: Semantic versioning writes every release as `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`. The number tells you if an update fixes a bug, adds a feature, or can break your code.

analogy.text: A textbook. A reprint fixes typos (patch), a revised edition adds chapters (minor), a rewrite changes the structure (major). Your notes survive only the first two.
analogy.breaks: Nothing enforces it: a maintainer can ship a breaking change as a patch.

points: Raising a number resets the ones to its right: minor bump `5.2.1` gives `5.3.0`.
`^5.2.1` accepts 5.2.1 up to, but not including, 6.0.0; `~5.2.1` stops before 5.3.0.
`npm install express` saves a `^` range; `package-lock.json` records the exact version.
`npm ci` installs exactly the versions in the lockfile, so every machine matches.

parts.label: Caret
parts.note: Accept newer minor and patch releases, never a new major.

parts.label: Major
parts.note: Raised when an update can break code that worked before.

parts.label: Minor
parts.note: Raised when a release adds features and stays backward compatible.

code.title: Bump a version
code.caption: Edit the version or the kind, then run again.

code.title: What a range accepts
code.caption: Each line: a version, then whether `^5.2.1` and `~5.2.1` accept it. A simplified matcher for 1.0.0 and above.

pitfalls: Packages below 1.0.0 may break on any minor: `^0.2.3` stops before 0.3.0.
Compare versions as three numbers, not text: `5.10.0` is newer than `5.9.0`.
Read the changelog before a major upgrade: Express 4 to 5 broke `app.get('*')`.

quiz.why: Raising minor resets patch to 0, giving 2.8.0. Raising major resets minor and patch, giving 3.0.0.

takeaway: A range says what you accept; the lockfile says what you got.
